claims.text: The simultaneous high strength and ductility of HEAs under dynamic loading arises from severe lattice distortion.
The random distribution of multiple principal elements causes severe lattice distortion in an HEA matrix.
Severe lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Severe lattice distortion promotes dislocation storage and multiplication during deformation.
Lattice distortion raises the energy barriers for dislocation movement, thereby increasing strength.
The complex energy landscape in HEAs promotes dislocation storage and multiplication, thereby enhancing ductility under dynamic loading.
Under identical dynamic-loading conditions, single-phase HEAs will have higher yield strength than conventional alloys with similar grain size and phase structure.
Under identical dynamic-loading conditions, single-phase HEAs will have greater uniform elongation than conventional alloys with similar grain size and phase structure.
The strength and uniform-elongation differences between HEAs and conventional alloys will increase as strain rate increases.
The hypothesis applies to single-phase HEAs having random solid-solution structures.
The hypothesis does not apply to HEAs with significant second-phase precipitation or ordered structures.
The proposed mechanism is valid at strain rates from approximately 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1.
The proposed mechanism is valid from room temperature to approximately 0.5 Tm.
Potential competing mechanisms include twinning and phase transformation.
The controlled comparison should use HEA and conventional-alloy specimens with matched grain size and phase structure, tested at 10^-3, 10^0, and 10^3 s^-1.
The hypothesis predicts a larger post-deformation increase in dislocation density in HEAs than in conventional alloys.

Failure of the HEA to show both higher yield strength and greater uniform elongation at every tested strain rate, or failure to show a larger dislocation-density increase, is specified as the falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome implies superior strength and uniform elongation throughout the tested dynamic-loading range and an increasing advantage at higher strain rates, whereas the stated rule only falsifies the hypothesis if no tested strain rate shows both advantages. Thus, failure at individual rates or failure of the predicted increasing rate trend would not falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
